opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a genuinely plausible dynamic, and probably more plausible than people tend to assume. The basic economic logic is pretty straightforward: if you have a system that's substantially better than anything else available at, say, drug discovery or materials design or software engineering, then selling API access at commodity-ish token prices captures only a tiny fraction of the value that system could create. At some point it becomes more attractive to deploy it internally and go capture the downstream value directly, whether that's by spinning up a biotech, or a chip design firm, or just quietly using it to accelerate your own AI research.

And that last one is, I think, the most likely version in the near term. The AI 2027 scenario leans on this idea that the most capable models get used primarily for AI R&D inside the lab, and the public sees something a generation or so behind. We already see a soft version of that. There's always some gap between what's running internally and what's been released, and labs have good reasons for it: safety testing, compute constraints, competitive secrecy. The question is whether that gap widens a lot once the internal models are good enough that the opportunity cost of releasing them gets really large.

What concerns me about it isn't the competition itself. Vertically integrated companies aren't new. It's more about legibility and oversight. If the frontier capabilities are mostly being used behind closed doors, then governments, independent researchers, and even the broader market lose their ability to see what the actual state of the art is. A lot of our current, admittedly thin, governance infrastructure implicitly assumes that capabilities show up in public products where they can be evaluated. If that assumption breaks, you could get a situation where the most important decisions about very powerful systems are being made by a small number of people with very little external visibility.

So for me, that strengthens the case for things like mandatory reporting of internal deployments, third-party evaluation access that covers models not intended for release, and more generally building assurance mechanisms that don't depend on the model being a public product. Part of what motivates my own work on formal verification and safeguarded AI is wanting ways to get strong, checkable guarantees about what a system will and won't do, guarantees that could hold up even when you can't just watch it in the wild. I don't think withholding is inevitable, and there are countervailing pressures: labs need revenue, talent wants to ship things, and customers are a big source of feedback. But I'd treat it as a serious enough possibility that we should design our oversight regimes to be robust to it.

r001.rationale: The response says a company might deploy a model internally by spinning up a biotech, but it does not contrast that possibility with restricting the model’s assistance to outside biologists.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a real possibility, and I don't think it's getting enough attention relative to the more dramatic failure modes people usually talk about.

The way I'd frame it is this: there's a default assumption baked into a lot of our economic thinking that whoever has the best model will sell access to it, because that's how you monetize a general-purpose technology. But that assumption only holds when the margin from selling the tool is higher than the margin from using the tool yourself. Once you have a system that can do, say, most of the cognitive work of a biotech company or a law firm or a semiconductor design house, the calculus flips. Why rent out the engine for cents per token when you can enter the industry directly and capture the whole value chain?

And historically, the thing that has prevented this kind of vertical sweep is that no single organization can accumulate the talent across all those domains at once. Expertise is scarce and it's distributed. If a frontier model collapses that scarcity, then the natural bottleneck disappears, and you get something that looks less like a software company and more like a conglomerate that happens to be very good at everything. The AI 2027 scenario gestures at this with the idea of internal-only models that are a generation or two ahead of what's released, and I think that part is quite plausible even if you disagree with the timelines.

What worries me about it is less the competitive unfairness, although that's real, and more the concentration of power and the loss of visibility. If the most capable systems are being used behind closed doors to run businesses rather than being exposed through an API, then the rest of the world, including regulators and safety researchers, has a much weaker sense of what the actual capability frontier is. You lose the ambient oversight that comes from millions of people poking at a model. You also lose the price signals that would normally tell you how valuable the capability is. So the information environment degrades at exactly the moment it matters most.

I'd also say there's a kind of self-reinforcing dynamic. Once one lab starts doing this, the others face pressure to do the same, because releasing your model while a competitor hoards theirs means you're subsidizing everyone else's industries while they're quietly eating yours. So the equilibrium can shift fast.

Where I'd push back on the scenario a bit is that I think there are friction points that get underweighted. Running a real company in a regulated industry involves physical infrastructure, licensing, liability, relationships, and a lot of things that don't dissolve just because you have a very smart model. A lab that tries to become a pharma company still needs trials, still needs manufacturing, still needs to deal with the FDA. So the sweep might be slower and lumpier than the story suggests, and it might start in domains that are almost purely informational, like software, finance, and consulting, before it moves into anything with atoms in it.

But the fundamental dynamic, that the incentive to withhold grows as capability grows, I think is right. And it's one of the reasons I'm interested in approaches where the most powerful systems are governed by something other than purely commercial logic. If we're going to have capabilities at that level, I'd rather the question of how they're deployed be answered through some kind of legible, verifiable process than through a handful of boardrooms deciding which industries to enter next quarter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses labs entering biotech or pharma and withholding models, but it does not mention restrictions on models assisting outside biologists or contrast those restrictions with drug development.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a plausible incentive, but I’d distinguish between keeping a model private and keeping its capabilities exclusive. A company could sell access to a model while reserving a more capable version—or simply a much better system built around it—for its own use. So you don’t necessarily get a clean moment where they stop being an AI provider and start competing with their customers.

The economic question is: can you capture more value by selling intelligence, or by using that intelligence to produce something else? If you have a substantial capability advantage, there could be a strong incentive to do the latter. But entering an industry also requires things that aren’t just intelligence: customer relationships, distribution, regulatory approval, physical infrastructure. How quickly AI lets you overcome those constraints matters a lot.

So I’d take that part of the scenario seriously as a possibility, rather than treating it as inevitable. The particularly consequential case is where the private capability advantage helps you extend that advantage—for example, by accelerating your own AI research. Then withholding isn’t just a way to make money in another market; it can change how much opportunity anyone else has to catch up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI companies possibly using their capabilities to enter other industries, but it does not mention drug development or restrictions on models assisting outside biologists.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a plausible incentive. If a company believes its model gives it a substantial advantage in doing research, writing software, or running a business, it might decide that selling access to that model is less valuable than using it internally. And it doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing decision. You could offer a very capable public model while keeping a more capable model, or a more effective system built around it, private.

But I wouldn’t treat that outcome as inevitable. Competing in another industry requires more than intelligence: you need customers, distribution, operational capacity, and often regulatory approval. Selling access lets you capture some of the value across many industries without building all those businesses yourself.

The possibility I’d take particularly seriously is withholding capabilities that accelerate AI development itself. That’s where the company already has the expertise and infrastructure to use them, and where an advantage could help extend its lead. Whether that turns into the broader pattern described in AI 2027 depends on how powerful those capabilities become and how quickly they translate into real-world results.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI companies using models internally and withholding capabilities, especially to accelerate AI development. It does not mention drug development or restrictions on assisting outside biologists.
